articles.title: A Nebraska man signed a two-page handwritten will leaving his estate to his longtime partner, but she wrote most of it herself; after his death, the state Supreme Court has ruled the document cannot replace his 1984 will
articles.summary: A handwritten will can offer a simple way to distribute property after death, but who actually writes its contents can determine whether it is legally
articles.body: A handwritten will can offer a simple way to distribute property after death, but who actually writes its contents can determine whether it is legally valid. In Nebraska, a dispute over a two-page handwritten document has ended with the state Supreme Court ruling that a man's signature was not enough to make the document a valid will when its important provisions had been written by someone else.In its October 30, 2026, opinion, available on Justia, the Nebraska Supreme Court upheld a lower court's ruling that a 2021 document could not replace Douglas G. Todd's original 1984 will. The dispute involved his longtime unmarried partner, Judy Sheets, who claimed that Todd had instructed her to write the document and had signed and dated it himself. However, she acknowledged that the material provisions were in her handwriting. The court held that this did not satisfy Nebraska's requirements for a handwritten, or holographic, will.A decades-long relationship and two competing willsThe case arose after Douglas Todd died in January 2025. His son, Chadd B. Todd, subsequently applied for informal probate of a will Douglas had signed in 1984. Under that document, Douglas had directed that all his property would go to his sons. However, Judy Sheets challenged the application, arguing that the 1984 document was no longer his last will. She claimed that Douglas had subsequently executed a two-page handwritten will in February 2021, leaving his estate to her.Sheets testified that she and Douglas had been in a long-term relationship for more than four decades, although they had never married. They had lived together as a couple until his death. She maintained that Douglas had personally signed and dated the 2021 document after telling her what to write. However, she acknowledged during her deposition that the remaining contents, including the provisions explaining how the property should be distributed, were entirely in her handwriting. The distinction became central to the probate dispute because several assets, including real estate and motor vehicles, were still titled solely in Douglas' name when he died.Both sides filed competing motions for summary judgment before the County Court for Lincoln County. The court ruled in favour of Chadd, finding that the 2021 document was not a valid holographic will because its material provisions were not written by Douglas. It also determined, as an alternative reason, that the document did not adequately express testamentary intent. Sheets appealed.Why the handwritten document failed Nebraska's legal requirementsThe Nebraska Supreme Court focused on the state's rules governing holographic wills. Under Nebraska Revised Statute Section 30-2328, a document that does not meet the usual requirements for a witnessed will may still be recognised as a holographic will, whether or not it is witnessed, if the testator's signature and material provisions are handwritten and the document includes a handwritten indication of the date of signing. The statute also provides limited exceptions where no date is indicated. This exception allows people to prepare wills without the formalities normally required for witnessed documents. However, it does not remove the requirement that the person making the will must write its essential provisions.Sheets argued that the 2021 document qualified because it was intended to be a joint will, meaning a testamentary document made by two people. She contended that both she and Douglas were testators, and therefore the handwriting requirement could be satisfied through her written contributions. The Supreme Court rejected this interpretation. It explained that a joint will, although contained in one document, effectively represents the separate wills of the individuals who sign it. Each person's wishes are treated as a separate testamentary disposition, and the document must be considered independently when one of the people dies.Consequently, even if the 2021 document represented both Sheets' and Douglas' wishes, only Douglas' individual will could be admitted in the probate proceedings concerning his estate. Since Douglas was the person whose property was being distributed after his death, the material provisions of the will offered for probate on his behalf had to be in his handwriting. Sheets' handwriting could not fulfil that requirement, even if she had accurately recorded the instructions he gave her.Court explains the purpose of holographic will rulesThe Supreme Court also considered decisions from other jurisdictions involving similar disputes over jointly prepared handwritten wills. It referred to earlier cases in which courts had concluded that a document written primarily by one person could not qualify as the holographic will of another person simply because the latter had signed it.The court noted that this interpretation was consistent with the purpose behind laws recognising handwritten wills. Holographic wills provide a relatively simple and inexpensive alternative to formally witnessed documents. However, requiring the testator to write the material provisions personally helps protect against fraud and provides an additional safeguard that the document reflects that person's actual wishes. Allowing someone else's handwriting to satisfy this requirement would weaken that protection, the court reasoned.The judges therefore concluded that the 2021 document could not be treated as Douglas' valid holographic will. Because this finding was sufficient to resolve the dispute, the Supreme Court did not need to examine the lower court's alternative conclusion about whether the document expressed testamentary intent.Nebraska Supreme Court upholds the earlier rulingThe Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed the County Court for Lincoln County's decision, leaving the 2021 handwritten document invalid as Douglas' holographic will. The ruling means that the document cannot supersede his 1984 will in the probate proceedings. The ruling leaves the 1984 will as the document governing the probate proceedings, under which Douglas had directed that his property go to his sons. The decision does not determine every possible issue concerning the estate or independently establish the ownership of each asset. It resolves the specific legal question of whether the 2021 document satisfied Nebraska's requirements for a holographic will.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine
articles.summary: Many Ukrainians, who have faced years of Russian attacks, did not take the messages seriously and doubted their veracity.
articles.body:
Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.

On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note – a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.

But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.

Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts.

"The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us."

"But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."

The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.

Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.

Anastasiia Romanytska, a 29-year-old ballerina living in Kyiv, said she does not have the alert app installed but friends forwarded her the warnings.

"My first reaction was, 'Is this some kind of joke?' But then my body reacted as if I was under stress. My heart started racing, and my stomach tightened up."

"Still, somehow I immediately realised that it wasn't something serious. Or maybe I just really wanted to believe that."

There are a number of apps delivering phone notifications of air raid warnings, with maps showing areas under threat, all using the same data as the official government-backed app.

Yevhen Baliutov, a cybersecurity expert at Kyiv School of Economics, told the BBC it was clear to him the Ukrainian alert system was hacked by Russians, saying many Ukrainians had clicked a link included with the alerts leading to a Russian Telegram channel, potentially exposing them to further disinformation, phishing attempts or data breaches.

"This is a war, so it's no surprise that Russia will try to hack, will try to send us fake news, will try to manipulate, and will use that for their propaganda."

While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.

Baliutov said it was also logical that Ukraine would have responded by launching a cyber-attack on the Russian emergency alert system. Both sides have similar capabilities in cyber warfare, he added.

Kochmar said after the initial concern, Ukrainians quickly turned to joking about the incident.

"All our work group chats immediately blew up. Everyone started messaging each other, discussing what was happening. And what I found fascinating was how quickly we turned the whole thing into a joke."

Although the impact of this incident had been limited, it illustrated the weakness of a crucial system, Baliutov said.

"It's very dangerous for Ukraine and for our people. When developing such applications, we need to consider security from the very beginning, without skipping essential security measures. When millions of people rely on a service, we cannot afford to take shortcuts with security."

The authorities already faced the challenge of maintaining public alertness after four and a half years of war with ceaseless attack warnings sounding sometimes hourly. Now they must reassure people the systems in place to protect them are robust, trustworthy and should be followed.

articles.title: Clifton and Vera Grover established an Alaska dairy farm in 1948; 115 acres have been permanently protected to keep the land in agricultural use
articles.summary: A farm established in Alaska in 1948 received permanent protection in June 2025.
articles.body: A farm established in Alaska in 1948 received permanent protection in June 2025. The 115.22-acre Grover Farm in Palmer, in the Matanuska Valley, was protected through a conservation easement agreed to by the Alaska Farmland Trust Corporation and the US Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service. The agreement ensures the property will remain in agricultural use.According to the US Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service (2025), Clifton and Vera Grover established the farm in the Matanuska Valley, where it became a family farming operation. It later moved from dairy production to cattle, while parts of the property were leased to other local farmers. The easement closed on June 13, 2025, securing the land against future development and preserving it for farming.How did Alaska Farmland Trust and NRCS protect 115 acres of Grover FarmThe conservation easement permanently protects 115.22 acres of Grover Farm in Palmer, Alaska. The Alaska Farmland Trust Corporation (AFTC) worked in partnership with the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) to secure the agreement. The agreement was completed on June 13, 2025, after five years of work between the Grover family and the AFTC.The voluntary agreement allows the family to keep ownership of the farm while receiving financial compensation for giving up its development rights permanently. The land can never be subdivided or paved over. Instead, it will remain available for farming, allowing future generations to continue using the property to grow food.From dairy farm to cattle operation and leased landClifton and Vera Grover established the farm in 1948 in Alaska’s Matanuska Valley. The farm has stood for more than seven decades as a family farm. It began as a dairy operation.Over time, the operation shifted to running cattle. The family also began leasing portions of the property to other local farmers, continuing its role in local food production.Wesley Grover, a longtime valley resident and farmland owner, said, “We came up in November of 1948 the first year we plowed all the land in oats and peas and vetch that we used for silage and hay. It is excellent soil. It is very important to learn how wonderful this soil is, this land here is excellent farmland.”Why Grover Farm’s location and soil matter amid development pressureThe easement came as the Matanuska-Susitna Valley was facing increasing development pressure.Margaret Adsit, lands coordinator for the AFTC, said, "Across the Valley, we’re seeing farmland converted into housing and non-agricultural uses.”"Once it’s gone, it’s gone for good. That’s why it’s crucial to act now."The Grover Farm easement is part of the trust’s efforts to safeguard agricultural land in the region. The agreement prevents the property from being subdivided or paved over, keeping it available for farming. The protected land is located close to markets and has about 15 feet of topsoil, according to the trust’s board president.How does Alaska’s FarmLink programme support new farmersThe Grover family continues to own the property under the conservation easement, while its development rights have been permanently retired. The agreement allows future farmers to grow food on the land. The project also forms part of the Alaska Farmland Trust Corporation’s wider work to preserve the state’s agricultural soils through voluntary conservation and farmer-centred land access programmes as part of its ongoing statewide conservation work.The organisation marked its 20th anniversary in 2025, when the Grover easement brought the total area it had conserved to 519 acres. The farm effort also aligns with its FarmLink programme, which connects farmland owners with aspiring farmers. articles.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to block 20,000 California ballots before midterms
articles.summary: California says any move to block ballots from suspected noncitizens could disenfranchise eligible US voters.
articles.body:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has asked the Supreme Court to stop California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are not US citizens.

The emergency request, filed on Monday, just one day before the US midterm elections , is the latest development in a legal battle between the administration and California, a Democratic stronghold and the most populous US state.

California says the move could disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.

The Department of Justice wants the Supreme Court to step in immediately and force California to set aside ballots from voters on a list compiled by the Department of Homeland Security until after their citizenship status can be verified.

The department argues that once the ballots are mixed in with others, there would be no way to identify them and remove them if the voters were later found to be ineligible.

But California says the list is unreliable and could include thousands of US citizens.

Voting has been under way since early October, with ballots mailed to around 23 million registered voters and hundreds of thousands already processed. State officials say it would be nearly impossible to separate the ballots in question.

Last week, a federal judge rejected the administration’s request, raising concerns about the reliability of the data on the list.

“If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Judge David Carter wrote.

The administration has turned to the Supreme Court after a federal appeals court also rejected the request on Friday.

It is not clear when the Supreme Court, which rejected an earlier effort to restrict mail-in voting in September, will rule. The case will be handled by Justice Elena Kagan, who hasn’t set a deadline yet for California to respond.

The dispute comes as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress in Tuesday’s elections.

Trump has repeatedly made false claims about widespread voter fraud, but studies and state audits have shown that ineligible voting, including by noncitizens, is rare.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy back in court seeking to have murder charges dismissed
articles.summary: Defence argues that retrying Clancy would violate ⁠⁠her constitutional rights.
articles.body:
Lindsay Clancy, the American mother facing murder charges for killing her three young children, has returned to court in a bid to get the charges dropped.

Clancy’s lawyers urged Judge William Sullivan on Monday to dismiss the first-degree murder charges against her in the state of Massachusetts in the United States, saying retrying her for killing her three young children would violate ⁠⁠her constitutional rights.

Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy if the case moves forward but have not decided if she would face the same first-degree murder charges.

Monday’s hearing was her second time in court since September, when jurors were unable to reach a verdict at her trial.

Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands in 2023 at her home in Duxbury, a suburb of Boston in Massachusetts. Clancy then attempted to take her own life by cutting herself with a knife and was paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window.

At Monday’s hearing, defence lawyer Martin G Weinberg argued that the judge should have investigated further after the jury foreperson sent two notes indicating that a juror was not following the rules. Further questioning could have revealed grounds to remove the juror, identified as Michael Desronvil, and continue deliberations, he said.

After receiving the notes, Sullivan spoke with each juror, reminding them of their duties and explaining what constitutes reasonable doubt in a court case. He asked whether they could apply the law to the case, and all said yes.

But Weinberg argued that Sullivan had not gone far enough. A juror who said he could follow the law could have been lying, Weinberg said, and the situation warranted questioning the foreperson separately to learn more about what was happening during deliberations.

Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague argued there was no indication the holdout juror’s disagreement stemmed from personal bias or an inability to deliberate, rather than a different assessment of the evidence.

Sprague said the judge handled the ⁠⁠jury impasse appropriately, saying the fact that one juror dug in his heels did not mean Sullivan should risk interfering with the deliberations by questioning him.

“It is clear from the record this ⁠⁠juror did not refuse to deliberate,” Sprague said. “He refused to agree.”

Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington accused the lone holdout juror of using a mobile phone to research terms related to the case and questioned whether he had been truthful during jury selection.

Clancy has never disputed killing her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behaviour. Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy, now 36, had mental health problems but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong.

Sullivan did not immediately rule on the motion to dismiss. He scheduled another hearing for November 16 and suggested a retrial could begin in March.

Another motion expected to be discussed is the state of Massachusetts’s request for a gag order barring lawyers and their supporters “from making extrajudicial statements to the media that would have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceeding”.

articles.title: Prosecutors hint at plans to retry Lindsay Clancy on murder charges
articles.summary: Judge William Sullivan said if the case is headed to a retrial, that could happen as soon as March 2027.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

Massachusetts prosecutors have given their clearest indication yet that they plan to retry Lindsay Clancy for the murder of her three children in 2023.

At a hearing on Monday, Judge William Sullivan scheduled a 16 November hearing where he plans to rule on a handful of motions that could determine how a retrial would proceed, including a request to dismiss the first-degree murder charges.

Clancy faced a weekslong trial on those charges over the summer. It fell apart in early September after a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.

If there is a retrial, Judge Sullivan said, it could happen as soon as March 2027.

The prosecution did not say on Monday whether Clancy would face the same charges or amended charges in the event of a retrial.

When the parties meet again later this month, they will hear the judge's rulings on the motions argued in court on Monday, and potentially will discuss dates for a retrial, Judge Sullivan said.

Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, pushed the judge for a spring trial.

"I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year or two or three," he said. "I want a date and I want it this spring."

But prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said she wants to hear Judge Sullivan's rulings on Monday's arguments before the prosecution commits to a new date or specifics for a potential retrial.

When the judge asked for more details on how prosecutors planned to proceed with a potential retrial, Sprague responded: "This would be a retrial - as to what that looks like will depend".

But that appeared to frustrate Reddington.

"Why do we not know if the next trial is going to be murder in the first degree or a lesser charge, why do they need to wait for the motions? I need to know logistically."

Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.

Prosecutors could decide to bring lesser charges against Clancy in a retrial. For example, second-degree-murder charges, apply to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning.

Despite Sprague's statement in court, District Attorney Timothy Cruz has not yet confirmed that Clancy will face a retrial and has not announced future plans for the case.

Much of Monday's conversations in court focused on the one holdout juror, also known as Juror Doe, and the defence's investigation into him. Juror Doe disagreed with the other jurors, who appeared to want to find Clancy not guilty by way of insanity. The lack of agreement led to a hung jury and mistrial.

In some of the most fiery moments of the three-hour hearing on Monday, Reddington requested a plethora of evidence including the holdout juror's phone and phone records.

Heather O'Connor, the attorney who represents Juror Doe, said she was in court because Clancy's defence team has "combined several allegations" to try to argue that a mistrial should not have been declared, she said.

That is among the motions Sullivan said he will rule on in a few weeks.

Clancy does not deny killing her children, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors claim the killings were intentional.

articles.title: Florida police unveil $148K flying patrol vehicle
articles.summary: Florida Polytechnic University's Jetson ONE eVTOL police vehicle named Astro still awaits FAA authorization before officers can fly operational patrols.
articles.body: You may be used to seeing police cars cruising through your neighborhood or helicopters flying overhead. But what if an officer could respond to an emergency in a small electric aircraft that looks like a giant drone? That idea is getting closer to reality in Florida. The Florida Polytechnic University Police Department in Lakeland has introduced a flying patrol vehicle that the university has nicknamed Astro. Jetson, the company behind the Jetson ONE personal flying machine, built the single-seat aircraft. According to the university, it's the first U.S. law enforcement agency to add this type of piloted electric aircraft to its fleet. Jetson calls it a world first. However, Astro still needs FAA authorization before officers can use it for operational police patrols. Here's how Astro works and why police believe this unusual aircraft could change the way they respond to emergencies. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FLYING SPORTS CAR HIDES ITS WINGS AS PRODUCTION GETS CLOSER Astro is Florida's new flying patrol vehicle Astro gets its name from the dog in the classic cartoon The Jetsons. The aircraft even looks like something George Jetson might have parked outside his house. Astro uses electric vertical takeoff and landing technology, commonly called eVTOL. As a result, it can lift straight into the air without needing a runway. Unlike a conventional police helicopter, Astro has a compact frame that folds for easier transport and storage. The aircraft features an open cockpit surrounded by a lightweight frame. Eight electric motors power its eight propellers. Meanwhile, a four-axis joystick allows the pilot to control its movement. Florida Polytechnic University selected the Jetson ONE to explore its potential for law enforcement. The aircraft arrived during summer 2026. Since then, police personnel have completed flight training, according to Jetson. That includes Police Chief Aaron Murray. Jetson also identifies the aircraft by its registration number, N911FP. The number references emergency services and Florida Polytechnic University. Jetson tells CyberGuy that Astro is a standard Jetson ONE with police lights added. Officers use a handheld radio, and the aircraft has mounts for action cameras. The company says a pilot-controlled searchlight could be added in the future. How fast can the flying police vehicle go? Astro may look compact, but its advertised performance is impressive. According to Jetson's published specifications, the aircraft can reach speeds of 63 mph. That's fast enough to cover short distances across a large campus without following roads or dealing with traffic. However, battery life limits how long it can stay airborne. Jetson estimates approximately 20 minutes of flight time per charge, making Astro better suited to short missions than extended patrols. Jetson tells CyberGuy that the aircraft takes approximately 90 minutes to recharge using a 240-volt connection. Charging through a standard household outlet takes about three hours. However, officers can swap batteries between flights. This allows them to return to the air sooner if fully charged replacements are available. Each flight still lasts approximately 20 minutes. Jetson confirms that the 210-pound maximum includes the pilot, police gear and any emergency supplies. The company says this is a hard limit, which could restrict how much equipment an officer can carry. Jetson also advertises several safety features. The company says Astro can continue flying even if one motor fails. It also has an automatic landing system and a ballistic parachute designed for emergencies. Jetson lists the vehicle at $148,000 before taxes and additional fees, making it a significant investment for a police department. How police could use Astro during emergencies Florida Polytechnic University wants to explore whether Astro can help officers respond when roads become difficult to navigate. Consider what happens after a major Florida storm. Roads may flood, debris can block access and emergency crews may struggle to reach certain locations. Once weather and flying conditions allow, a small aircraft that takes off vertically could help officers survey the damage. Police Chief Aaron Murray believes Astro could help officers monitor the campus and reach places that traditional vehicles cannot easily access. The department also wants to investigate using it to deliver emergency supplies. "Advanced air mobility is a technology on the rise, and we can either choose to be proactive or reactive as it develops," Murray said. The university also plans to collaborate with regional law enforcement agencies on potential emergency-response missions. However, Astro carries only its pilot. It cannot transport an injured person or bring someone back from a rescue mission. Because the 210-pound limit includes the officer and everything onboard, the amount of emergency supplies Astro can carry depends on the pilot's weight and equipment. PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE The FAA hurdle facing Florida's flying police vehicle There's an important regulatory issue before Astro can become a regular part of police operations. Jetson developed the ONE as a recreational aircraft designed around the FAA's Part 103 ultralight rules. Those rules allow qualifying ultralight vehicles to operate without traditional aircraft or pilot certification. However, Part 103 limits their use to recreational or sporting purposes. Police patrols fall outside those permitted uses. FAA guidance specifically identifies aerial surveying and patrolling as activities that cannot operate under Part 103. Jetson says Florida Polytechnic University needs additional federal authorization involving FAA Part 91 rules to use Astro for public-safety missions. When the university announced the aircraft in mid-October, it said the approval process was in its final stages. At that time, officials expected approval in November or December. The university has not publicly confirmed when regular operational police patrols will begin. Students will help develop the flying police aircraft's future Astro has another role beyond its potential police duties. It will serve as a hands-on research platform for Florida Polytechnic University students. The university launched an aerospace engineering degree program in fall 2026. As a result, students will have an opportunity to study electric aircraft technology while learning about the challenges of operating it. Faculty members and students plan to use Astro's flight data for research and senior engineering projects. Reports also indicate that the university is exploring virtual training simulations for police officers. This could provide useful information about how small electric aircraft perform during specialized missions. It may also help future engineers identify limitations that need attention before wider adoption. Florida is also expanding its involvement in advanced air mobility. The nearby SunTrax transportation testing facility in Auburndale has a dedicated aerial test track for emerging aircraft technology. Testing under Florida's participation in a federal advanced air mobility pilot program is expected to begin by the end of 2026. That statewide testing effort is separate from Astro's pending authorization for police operations. Could more police departments start using flying vehicles? Astro raises an interesting possibility for law enforcement agencies looking for alternatives to traditional helicopters. Police helicopters require significant resources to purchase and maintain. A smaller electric aircraft could eventually offer another option for certain missions, especially when an officer needs a quick view of an area from above. However, Jetson's aircraft also has substantial limitations. Its short flight duration means officers would need to plan missions carefully. Swappable batteries could support repeated flights, but officers would still need to land between missions to replace them. Weather conditions and airspace restrictions could further affect operations. There's also the question of whether a single-seat piloted aircraft provides enough benefits compared with a drone, which can conduct aerial surveillance without putting an officer in the cockpit. Even so, Jetson sees the police department's purchase as an important step toward expanding personal electric aircraft into professional use. The company says its entire 2026 and 2027 production is sold out. It is now accepting orders for 2028, with a listed price of $148,000. Jetson also expects Astro to appear at the public UP.Summit event at Kennedy Space Center in Florida on November 7 and 8. What this means to you You probably won't see flying patrol vehicles operating above your neighborhood anytime soon. However, Astro offers an early look at how public-safety agencies might use small electric aircraft. After a major storm, an officer flying over blocked roads could potentially assess damage and help emergency crews understand where assistance is needed. The same technology might eventually support searches for missing people, although Astro's usefulness still needs to be demonstrated during actual police operations. There's another side worth considering. As police departments explore aerial technology, questions about privacy will become increasingly important. People may want to know when officers can fly above their property and whether aircraft will collect or record information. Those questions deserve attention alongside the aircraft's potential benefits. For now, Florida Polytechnic University has an opportunity to study a new approach to emergency response while working toward the necessary federal authorization. Kurt's key takeaways I've been following Jetson's flying aircraft for several years, and seeing one enter a police department's fleet is an interesting development. When I first covered the Jetson ONE, the attraction was the idea of people being able to fly their own electric aircraft. Now we're seeing a possible use beyond recreation. I can understand why a police department would want this technology, especially in Florida, where storms can leave communities cut off from emergency services. But I'm also interested in what happens after the excitement wears off. Twenty minutes of flight time leaves little room for unexpected delays, and there's still the question of whether an officer flying overhead offers enough advantages over a drone to justify the expense. I'm encouraged that the university plans to study those questions before putting Astro into regular service. And I think communities should have a say in how police use these aircraft, particularly when it comes to privacy. Would seeing police officers flying above your neighborhood make you feel safer, or would you worry about having another set of eyes watching from the sky? articles.body: Matt Rhule knows the coaching world will test your ability to keep moving forward during difficult times. But when someone involves your family, a line has been crossed — one that is difficult to explain to those who did not sign up for the job. We see it far too often. FLORIDA STATE FIRES MIKE NORVELL AFTER FAN REVOLT, CLEMSON LOSS SPARKS DECISION TO PAY MASSIVE BUYOUT While Matt Rhule is fair game for criticism when Nebraska loses or fails to perform on the field, targeting his family is completely unacceptable. articles.title: Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president
articles.summary: The case, part of the "Farmgate" scandal, has left President Cyril Ramaphosa mired in an impeachment saga.
articles.body:
A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $500,000 (£372,822) in cash from a farm owned by South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.

Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.

Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.

Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.

David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking $580,000 (£432,000) in cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.

David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.

Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.

There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.

The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.

Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.

An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.

articles.title: Russia bombs aid center and shelter in southern Ukraine, killing 26, officials say
articles.summary: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia bombed an aid distribution center and neighboring shelter in southern Ukraine on Monday, killing 26 people, Ukrainian officials said.
articles.body: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia bombed an aid distribution center and neighboring shelter in southern Ukraine on Monday, killing 26 people, Ukrainian officials said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X that 10 guided bombs targeted an area that included a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid and a nearby shelter. “This is further proof that Russia wants no de-escalation,” Zelenskyy said. The attacks in the village of Komyshuvakha, in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, occurred as a limited ceasefire expired Monday in Kherson, a different region in the country’s south. The limited ceasefire agreement had allowed humanitarian aid and evacuation missions into front-line areas in Russian-occupied territory. “There was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible,” Zelenskyy said. “With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings.” As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used flashlights to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials. About 20 people are considered missing and the death toll could rise, these officials say. Efforts to rescue people Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia. In other areas of Ukraine, authorities reported multiple Russian drone attacks that injured at least 17 people. After cyberattacks, false alerts sent in Ukraine and Russia Earlier, residents of Ukraine and Russia had received phony emergency alerts from government-run mobile apps that were hacked, authorities in both countries said. The phony alerts in Ukraine included a warning about an imminent nuclear threat. It was not clear if the cyberattacks late Sunday in Ukraine and early Monday in Russia were related. Ukraine said its mobile app, which residents rely on to seek safety from Russian missile and drone strikes, was up and running again after being temporarily suspended. Russian authorities said efforts to restore its emergency alert mobile app were ongoing. A Russian Telegram channel with links to the country’s security services said Monday that a hacking group, Hitcore, claimed responsibility for the breach of the Ukrainian emergency alert system. The Associated Press did not independently verify the claim, and the affiliations or motivations of the purported hackers remained unclear. The alerts received by Ukrainians — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv — were written in English, Russian and Ukrainian. The English language alerts contained spelling and grammatical errors. One of the messages, written in Russian, said: “Hi! There will be a nuclear threat across Ukraine. Do not worry, the Oreshnik is incoming,” a reference to a Russian ballistic missile. There was little indication the fake alerts caused panic in Ukraine. Instead, there was a flood of humorous posts online, with social media users sharing photos of their pets relaxing and apocalypse-themed images generated by artificial intelligence. A spokesman for Ukraine’s air force command, Yurii Ihnat, said in a television interview that the cyberattack had no impact on Ukraine’s security and defense operations. The government urged people to monitor other emergency channels on social media while the cyberattack was being addressed. In Russia, the Emergency Situations Ministry said in a statement that hackers sent a false alert through its app at approximately 2:45 a.m. Moscow time on Monday across 33 of Russia’s 89 regions. It did not say who it believed carried out the attack. The ministry sought to reassure Russians by noting that the wider public alert system was working normally through SMS messages, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers. “All government bodies must take steps to improve the cybersecurity of our digital resources,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said. Limited ceasefire ends in Kherson region As the ceasefire in Ukraine’s Kherson region came to an end on Monday, Ukraine’s general staff said that Russia’s military had used the pause in fighting to bolster its drone defenses and replenish ammunition supplies. The brief pause in fighting, which began on Oct. 27, was part of a humanitarian aid and evacuation mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, and marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion began nearly five years ago. Elsewhere in Ukraine, emergency services reported that drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region and damaged a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and residential buildings. Five people were also reported injured in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, where a warehouse was targeted and homes were damaged. Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Monday that it shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight. The head of Russia’s Samara region, Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, said in a statement that local air defenses were repelling an aerial attack, but did not give further details. Independent Russian media outlets later reported that Ukrainian drones had targeted one of Europe’s largest oil transport hubs in Samara.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos’ fund gave Mary’s Place $5 million in 2020; five years later, a case study records 2,668 families securing stable housing and more than 6,000 receiving shelter and outreach support
articles.summary: A $5 million grant from Jeff Bezos’ Day 1 Families Fund in 2020 has helped Seattle-based nonprofit Mary’s Place strengthen its efforts to support families
articles.body: A $5 million grant from Jeff Bezos’ Day 1 Families Fund in 2020 has helped Seattle-based nonprofit Mary’s Place strengthen its efforts to support families experiencing homelessness. Five years later, the organisation has helped 2,668 families secure safe and stable housing, while more than 6,000 families have received assistance through emergency shelter and mobile outreach services, according to a case study published in December 2025.For more than two decades, Mary’s Place has been working towards its mission of ensuring that no child sleeps outside. Based in Seattle, Washington, the nonprofit provides emergency shelter, mobile outreach and homelessness prevention services, while partnering with other organisations in the community to help families find a way out of homelessness.Its mission also inspired the establishment of the Bezos Day 1 Families Fund, which supports organisations working to address family homelessness.How Jeff Bezos’ $5 million grant helped Mary’s PlaceMary’s Place received its first $5 million grant from the Bezos Day 1 Families Fund in 2020. The funding allowed the organisation to expand its homelessness diversion programme, which helps families explore alternative housing arrangements and avoid entering emergency shelters whenever possible.A significant part of the investment went towards strengthening its partnerships with landlords and property owners to help families secure stable accommodation. The grant also enabled Mary’s Place to increase staffing capacity at its Family Center in The Regrade, which opened in an Amazon office building in 2020 and remains the organisation's largest shelter.The additional resources proved particularly important during the COVID-19 pandemic, when an unprecedented number of families approached the organisation for immediate assistance. With increased demand for emergency accommodation, Mary’s Place expanded its capacity to respond to the crisis and help families transition into permanent housing.According to the December 2025 case study, the organisation assisted 2,668 families in securing safe and stable housing during the five-year grant period. More than 6,000 families were also served through its emergency shelter and mobile outreach programmes.CEO Dominique Alex said the organisation's first grant helped it respond to the unexpected needs of families during the pandemic and play a leading role in the community during an exceptionally difficult period."Our first Day 1 Families Fund grant in 2020 allowed us to meet the unanticipated needs of families during the pandemic and be a leader in our community during this difficult crisis," Alex said.Mary’s Place plans to expand its services with its 2025 grantDespite the progress, homelessness remains a major challenge across the Seattle region, with shelters operating at full capacity.With its 2025 Day 1 Families Fund grant, Mary’s Place plans to pilot an Intensive Acute Outreach Program to reach families with complex needs, including those living in cars, tents and other precarious situations.The organisation also plans to invest in 200 shelter beds with wraparound services for families experiencing homelessness. It will further expand housing navigation services and flexible funding options to help more families find permanent accommodation.Alex said the organisation had learnt valuable lessons from its pandemic response and was now better positioned to reach families in difficult circumstances."We can’t do it alone; we need our community to come alongside us," she said, describing the collective effort as "the magic of Mary’s Place".Reflecting on the organisation's future, she added, "We’ve learned so much. We’re in a position to meet families where they are and help them find stability. Ending family homelessness is possible—but it takes all of us."How Mary’s Place helped a mother and daughter rebuild their livesThe December 2025 case study also highlights the experience of Paula, a military veteran who found herself homeless with her five-year-old daughter, Alayla, after a series of devastating setbacks.After leaving an unhealthy marriage, Paula and her daughter had moved to Louisiana to start afresh. However, two hurricanes destroyed their home, leaving Paula with little to rebuild their lives. Determined to find a new beginning, she travelled to Seattle in search of employment and housing.Initially, she managed to keep them in a motel while looking for work and permanent accommodation. But when her money ran out, she found herself without anywhere to go."I just started calling places and saying, ‘Hey, I’m sitting outside of a motel on the street with my daughter, she’s five, we have nowhere to go,’" Paula recalled.One of those calls connected her with Mary’s Place. Within hours, the organisation arranged transportation and welcomed Paula and Alayla into its 24-hour family shelter.The support went beyond providing them with a roof over their heads. While Alayla benefited from a trauma-informed environment, youth services and the opportunity to connect with other children, Paula worked with housing specialists to secure permanent accommodation.Today, the mother and daughter have a stable home. Reflecting on the support they received, Paula said, "She’s resilient, she’s strong, and she’s beautiful, and we got through it together. The staff at Mary’s Place were so caring. I always tell them they gave me my life back."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.summary: Angela Rayner previously said plans were "un-British" and ministers shouldn't shift "the goalposts".
articles.body:
Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.

When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.

But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.

But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.

Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.

Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.

Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".

She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.

That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.

For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.

Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.

All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.

In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.

But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.

Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches when Mahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier .

Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnel and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.

Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers

What are the planned changes to immigration rules?

Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.

One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.

They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.

One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.

Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.

Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.

Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.

The social care workers plans announced today will see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed , that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.

In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.

She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.

They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.

But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

articles.title: Australian developer who illegally cleared hundreds of native trees seeks approval for a $9.85 million Sydney mansion with a bowling alley, infinity pool and underground car park
articles.summary: An Australian property developer who illegally cut down hundreds of native trees in Sydney has submitted a fresh application to build a mansion worth
articles.body: An Australian property developer who illegally cut down hundreds of native trees in Sydney has submitted a fresh application to build a mansion worth nearly $10 million on the same property. Amir Abu Abara owns a 7.4-hectare site in Barden Ridge, where he previously cleared vegetation without development approval to make way for a $3 million mansion.He was fined $70,000 after Sutherland Shire Council agreed to drop a two-year court case in July 2025. The developer had also agreed to restore the environmentally sensitive land by replanting thousands of plants, including native trees. According to ABC News, his latest application includes plans for another mansion, a swimming pool and road access, while proposing further tree removal.New $9.85 million mansion plan includes bowling alley and underground car parkIn early March 2026, Abu Abara lodged a new development application for a mansion, swimming pool and road access at his Barden Ridge property. The proposed development has an estimated value of $9,853,863. Its architectural drawings and concept design are the same as those included in an earlier application submitted in 2023, which was rejected.The plans include several luxury facilities inside the proposed property. These are a tenpin bowling alley, an indoor basketball court, a gym with a sauna, an infinity pool and a movie theatre. The design also features a prayer room, a man-cave, a library and an underground car park with six spaces. The proposal includes a 160-metre-long driveway that would require the removal of 23 additional trees.What environmental concerns have residents raised over the mansion proposalThe proposed development has drawn criticism from residents nearby. Iris Freeman, secretary of the Woronora River Community Association, said residents were “angry, sad and very frustrated” that Abu Abara was preparing another application instead of restoring the cleared vegetation.She said, "Is that not just a slap in the face, and that really is a complete disregard for the environment and for the law.”An environmental report found that the property was on environmentally sensitive land and was home to threatened species, including koalas and powerful owls.Abu Abara agrees to restore vegetation after unauthorised tree clearingThe earlier unauthorised clearing was carried out to make way for a six-bedroom, eight-bathroom mansion valued at $3 million for Abu Abara and his wife, Caroline Abara. As part of a signed enforceable undertaking, the developer agreed to return the land to the condition it was in before the clearing.The restoration plan requires the planting of 38,700 plants, including 600 native trees. The work is to be completed within 18 months of July 2025. Abu Abara also submitted an apology to the court as part of the undertaking. He accepted that his conduct was wrong, apologised and said he hoped to undo the distress caused to the community. The undertaking also set out the conditions for restoring the site.What role does the vegetation management plan play in the mansion applicationSutherland Shire Council said it could not prevent a property owner from submitting a development application for land they own. It said the new proposal would be assessed on its merits. The council also said any development would depend on the owner meeting the vegetation management plan's requirements, including replanting the area affected by the illegal clearing.The council had issued Abu Abara a $30,000 fine in February after finding that he had failed to complete agreed sediment and erosion control measures. In late March, it issued a further $45,000 penalty notice over what it described as his continued failure to carry out remediation work to protect the nearby Woronora River.You use AI every day. articles.title: Merthyr woman told she had anxiety but it was breast cancer
articles.summary: Beth Jenkins' cancer was initially missed after told she was "too young" to have the disease.
articles.body:
A woman who said she was told by a GP she may be experiencing "medical anxiety" after finding a lump in her breast was later diagnosed with cancer.

Beth Jenkins, 42, visited a locum GP at her practice with concerns that a lump on her right breast had grown significantly and said she was told she was "too young to have breast cancer" and it may be linked to postnatal depression instead.

However, it was lobular breast cancer , with a 5cm (2in) tumour and the disease had spread to three lymph nodes.

Practice 1 Keir Hardie Health Park said it could not discuss individual cases but encouraged patients to "make a second appointment" if they had concerns about their health or care.

The mum-of-two, from Merthyr Tydfil, first noticed a "small pea-sized" lump in her breast in 2018, but, after an ultrasound, she was told it was likely glandular tissue and no biopsy was carried out.

A few years later she had given birth to her daughter Robyn and, while changing her nappy, Robyn accidentally kicked the right side of her chest.

It was then Jenkins noticed the lump had become "massive" so she visited her GP practice in October 2024.

She said, being 40 at the time, she was told she was "too young" to have breast cancer and the lump may be linked to an infection or "medical anxiety" as she had postnatal depression, and was prescribed antibiotics.

She said: "I haven't got medical anxiety, otherwise I'd be up the hospital and doctors' every week."

Two weeks later she returned to the practice while taking her baby for an appointment and decided to speak to a female GP about her concerns.

The GP reviewed her notes and advised her to submit an e-consult, saying she should have been referred straight away.

"So I went straight home, did what she said and the same locum doctor picked it up and he rang me," she said.

"He was like, 'you're still a bit anxious about this lump here.' I said, 'I'm not anxious. I said it's something, it's non-infection. I need to have it seen to'."

She was referred to a breast clinic and diagnosed on 14 November 2024 - the cancer had spread to three lymph nodes by the time it was found.

"Me and my dad, we just sat in shock really. I didn't even cry, I didn't get upset," she said.

Despite the devastating news, Jenkins, a police officer, praised the specialist team, saying the consultant reassured her: "I promise you I will get rid of this."

At first, Jenkins had a mastectomy and initially told her eight-year-old daughter Fallon that she had a "boob job".

She laughed: "Her remark to me was, 'why did you just have the one boob done and not the other one'?"

Jenkins decided to tell Fallon she had cancer before starting chemotherapy and radiotherapy - which caused her to lose her hair.

She had further preventative treatment, but experienced serious complications including neutropenic sepsis .

"They said if I had gone there [to the hospital] 24 hours later, I wouldn't have survived," she said.

Jenkins is classed as having no evidence of disease but will be monitored for 15 years.

She said people have described her as "one of the lucky ones" but added: "Lucky would be not to have cancer at all, and not for my kids to see what they've had to see for the last two years."

Jenkins described GPs as "the gateway to the services" and "if you can't get past the GP to get to that service, there's people dying".

In the UK, routine NHS breast screening is not automatically offered to 40-year-olds, as standard invitations begin at 50.

Dr Lee Campbell from Cancer Research Wales said, although uncommon, there were about 100-115 cases of breast cancer in women under 40 each year in Wales.

"Age should not be a deciding factor for referral for further investigations if symptoms present in younger women," he added.

Jenkins hopes sharing her story will encourage others to "keep pushing" for answers and to fight to be heard.

"If I hadn't had a voice, or if I'd just listened to that doctor, I could be sitting here now and they'd say, 'it's in your bones, in your brain'," she said.

"So many more people are sat in the house right now who should have been diagnosed and by the time they go back they're terminal.

"Cancer didn't care that I was a mother to a 10 month old... cancer doesn't discriminate".

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines state that people 40 and under should be referred for further investigation if they have an unexplained breast or armpit lump, with or without pain, or skin changes that could indicate breast cancer.

Research by Cancer Research Wales found "an inequity" on how GPs apply these - some following them closely while others rely on experience or instinct.

Campbell said: "We are currently working with researchers and primary care centres across Wales to ensure guidelines are followed and best practice is pursued.

"With respect to cancer, this will enable GP practices to go from gatekeepers to case-finders and will ensure cases like Beth's are dealt with sooner and not readily dismissed."

Since raising concerns publicly, Jenkins said her GP practice had been "pretty forthcoming" and put out a statement on social media in July 2025.

It said a "serious diagnosis was unfortunately missed at first.

"Thankfully, she returned to see another member of our team who sent an urgent referral - but had they not, the outcome could have been very different. In the patient's own words 'trust your instincts'."

Jenkins said she had "tried to turn a negative into a positive."

To mark two years since her diagnosis, she decided to create Breast Fest, a charity event to raise money for Merthyr Cancer Aid on 14 November that has raised £6,000 from ticket sales alone.

"People are being so kind. It's gone really well and I'm hoping to raise a lot of money," she said.

articles.title: The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special teased in new photos
articles.summary: Little has been shared about the plot of the upcoming The Other Bennet Sister Christmas special.
articles.body:
New images have been revealed ahead of the Christmas special of BBC series The Other Bennet Sister.

Inspired by Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, the first series was filmed largely in Wales and attracted 6.5 million UK viewers in its first 28 days.

The series finale saw Mary Bennet, played by Ella Bruccoleri, agree to marry Tom Hayward, played by Donal Finn.

Filming wrapped on the three-part Christmas special at the end of August.

Little has been shared about the plot of the upcoming episodes, but the BBC teased: "With marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs Hayward?" as fans eagerly await its return.

The first series of The Other Bennet Sister focused on Mary, the oft-overlooked middle sister in Pride and Prejudice, as she navigates the societal pressures of Regency England where marriage is both an aspiration and a necessity.

It was mostly filmed in south Wales at locations including Merthyr Mawr in Bridgend county, the Gower peninsula, and Brecon, in Powys.

The Christmas special has been produced by Cardiff-based Bad Wolf, and filming took place over the summer, also primarily in Wales .

Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones returns to the hit show as Mrs Bennet, who she previously described as "often quite cruel" to her daughter.

Other returning cast members include Ted Lasso's Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley and Laurie Davidson as Mr Ryder.

Also resuming their roles are Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham and Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock.

Nerys Amber-Stocks, best known for appearing in Out There and Mammoth, joins the cast as Mary's housemaid Lucy.

The stills also reveal another look at Bruccoleri and Finn, and the BBC teased: "Just as Mary begins this new chapter, an unexpected visitor from her past arrives at her door in need of her help..."

The show's producer Edoardo Ferretti had previously announced to fans on social media that the special had finished filming at the end of August.

He posted a short message on Instagram, saying: "And yet another wrap! Every time emotional, every time proud. This one is going to be so special!"

The three additional episodes, announced in June , will run for 30 minutes each and continue to be based on storylines from the original novel by Janice Hadlow.

It has been written by screenwriter Sarah Quintrell, who wrote nine of the series' 10 episodes, while Asim Abbasi returns to direct the special.

It will air in the UK on BBC iPlayer and BBC One, while in the US and Canada, it will also be available on BritBox.

articles.title: Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
articles.summary: Governments in Singapore and Malaysia are split between anxious citizens and an irascible neighbour.
articles.body:
The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.

Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.

It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.

"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."

Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.

But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.

Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.

In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".

There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.

"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.

"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."

Singapore's government, for its part, has made it clear that the haze problem is a priority.

Hundreds of haze shelters have been set up across the island, and masks are being distributed to children, the elderly and other vulnerable residents.

Authorities have also said they're looking to strengthen existing haze legislation and are investigating 10 Singapore-registered companies for potential links to the wildfires in Indonesia.

Last week, Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta for what the former described as "honest" and "sincere" conversations that produced "constructive approaches".

The meeting came as both countries announced they would set up a joint task force to deal with the haze - an apparent détente after weeks of simmering bilateral tensions.

As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism .

One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".

That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.

"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.

"The Indonesian public is suffering as well , and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."

Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.

To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.

But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.

"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.

"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."

In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.

Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".

For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.

It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.

The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.

But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.

The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.

"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."

In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.

Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.

Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.

In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side.

"As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.

And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.

For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh.

"The government is just wringing their hands till the wind blows [the problem] over. Because eventually it will blow over."

articles.title: Trump approval rating near record low on eve of US midterm elections: Poll
articles.summary: Only 32 percent of voters approve of Trump’s job performance in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.
articles.body:
Ahead of the United States midterm elections , President Donald Trump’s job approval rating continues to sit near a record low, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.

Some 32 percent of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the presidency, 1 percentage point above his rating two weeks ago.

Meanwhile, the Republican Party continues to be unpopular among those polled: When asked whether they would vote for a generic Democrat or Republican candidate, 46 percent of respondents preferred Democrats compared with 38 percent preferring Republicans.

Trump himself is not on the ballot, but he has repeatedly told his supporters to vote as if they are voting for him. If the Republican Party loses control of the US Congress, Trump has warned, Democrats may seek to impeach him for a third time.

Trump’s approval rating has dropped steadily, polls suggest, especially since the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28. The conflict has driven up petrol and diesel prices and has had secondary effects for US consumers worried about inflation and the economy.

The president embarked on a nearly monthlong campaign blitz ahead of the November 3 midterms in an effort to shore up support for Republican candidates, who are trying to retain control of the US House of Representatives and Senate.

Trump wrapped up his campaigning on Monday afternoon with a rally in Washington, DC, at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The president has devoted significant attention to the site as part of his attempt to renovate the capital. The job ran months late and cost more than 10 times its original estimate, with a special liner for the pool that Trump touted peeling away soon after it was installed.

“It was a work of art that never worked, but now it will work,” Trump said at the rally. He spent much of his speech on his renovation plans for the city, including a “Triumphal Arch”, which is facing legal challenges .

Trump seemed to acknowledge on Monday that his campaigning might not deliver the results he wants for his party, but said this was the political norm for midterm elections.

“For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms,” Trump said. “But we gave this a very strong shot.”

articles.title: First in 47 years: No operational fatality in CRPF in an entire year
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: CRPF has completed a year without a single operational fatality for the first time in 47 years, despite high-risk deployments across Jammu &
articles.body: NEW DELHI: CRPF has completed a year without a single operational fatality for the first time in 47 years, despite high-risk deployments across Jammu & Kashmir, Left-wing extremism-hit areas and Manipur."A significant milestone in the history of CRPF - 12 consecutive months have passed without any operational fatality, the last operational fatality being on Oct 30, 2025," CRPF DG G P Singh said Monday. He credited the milestone to modern hardware, better training, strategic planning and high-speed evacuation of injured personnel to medical facilities.CRPF personnel led the battle against LWE in 2026, hitting Maoists in pocket boroughs and eliminating their leadership. In Manipur, CRPF is deployed since violence broke out there in 2023. The state continues to face bouts of violence, many over the past one year..Since 1947, 2,268 CRPF men have been killed in operations, averaging over 28 fatalities a year. The highest toll was 143 in 2010, largely due to a Maoist ambush that killed 75 personnel.A CRPF official attributed zero fatalities to course-correction. Operations are planned, personnel get protective gear, and routine movements in high-risk areas are treated like operational movements. Also, 1.5 times the required force is deployed. "There was not a single casualty during Op Black Forest in Kareguttalu Hills last year, even as 21 Naxalites were killed," he added.A post-analysis found that three-fourths to four-fifths of fatalities occur days after injury. Timely medical care could prevent such deaths, the officer said, adding that air ambulances take injured personnel to advanced hospitals.This is the sixth time CRPF has recorded nil fatal casualties.
